nodes.question: What is the main goal of the circular economy in terms of resource use?
nodes.answer: The main goal of the circular economy is to reduce waste generation and promote the sustainable use of resources.

By 2050, the world population is expected to grow to 10 billion (UN 2022), which could further worsen the current situation by increasing pressure on the ecosystem to meet human needs (Ciliberto et al. 2021; Voukkali et al. 2023). To address these global challenges, the concept of the circular economy is gaining increasing importance as it can foster the achievement of more sustainable development (Geissdoerfer et al. 2017; Prieto-Sandoval et al. 2018; van Langen et al. 2021). The circular economy is a production and consumption model intended to reduce waste genera- tion and promote the sustainable use of resources (Kirchherr et al. 2017; Sica et al. 2022). Unlike the traditional linear economy based on the take-make-dispose model, the cir - cular economy focuses on building regenerative systems by closing loops (Farooque et al. 2019 ; Aithal and Aithal 2023; Bocken et al. 2023). nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What does the circular economy aim to achieve in relation to emissions?
nodes.answer: The circular economy aims to efficiently allocate wastage in energy production, secure environmental quality, and fill out the energy shortage.
nodes.paragraph: The European Union recently declared that half of total emissions come from daily wastage by productive & non- productive activities. In such a scenario, the circular economy has become the last resort to solve this issue by efficiently allocating wastage in energy production 21. This initiative not only tries to secure the environmental quality but also fills-out the energy shortage. The current study aims to describe the overall environmental challenges (income, urbanization & natural resources) and their best solutions (renewable energy, ICT & circular economy) for the top waste re-utilize economies (WRE) from 2000 to 2021. It is imperative to introduce this study S contribution to existing literature properly. Firstly , this study considers income a determinant of environmental degradation because most economies have tried to speed up their development plans to compete with other nations at any cost of negative externalities. It S a common belief that economies damage their available natural and other resources connected with sustainability and development plans, bringing severe environmental deterioration with rapid economic growth. Also, the present study offers a comparative analysis by using the load capacity factors as an alternative proxy of explained variables to demonstrate the shape of the load capacity curve (LCC) in specified economies.

nodes.question: What is the relationship between economic growth and natural resource use in the context of the circular paradigm?
nodes.answer: The circular paradigm aims to reduce the need for new resource extraction, thus decoupling economic growth from the intensive use of natural resources.

In this perspective, the circular paradigm contributes to decoupling economic growth from the intensive use of natural resources (Chen et al. 2020 ; Lei et al. 2021 ), thus contributing to the sustainable development goals (SDGs). Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is among the most widely adopted methodologies for quantifying the environmen- tal impacts of products or services throughout their entire lifecycle, providing a robust basis for environmental sus- tainability assessments and circular economy strategies (Hellweg and Mil i Canals 2014; ISO 2020a; Lei et al. 2021; Br ndstr m and Saidani 2022; Sica et al. 2022). LCA consists of four main steps, namely, goal and scope definition, Life Cycle Inventory (LCI), Life Cycle Impact Assessment (LCIA), and interpretation of results (ISO 2020a; ISO 2020b). nodes.answer: The inner loop type in the circular economy loop dimension includes the three inner loops from the butterfly diagram by EMF, 2013.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Waste reduction strategies|Circular economy_qna_004
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How does incentivizing repair in the inner loop of the CE Loop contribute to a circular economy?
nodes.answer: By encouraging repair and longer use of clothing items, the inner loop of the CE Loop ensures that resources are utilized efficiently and items are kept in circulation for as long as possible, reducing waste and promoting sustainability.

nodes.question: What is the aim of the circular economy according to the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The aim of the circular economy is to extend the life of products and materials to reduce waste, thereby maintaining their highest utility and value, and to create an economy that minimizes the intake of virgin materials and waste generation.

nodes.question: What does the circular economy aim to achieve in terms of waste and resource management?
nodes.answer: The circular economy aims to extend the life of products and materials to reduce waste, maintain their highest utility and value, minimize the intake of virgin materials, and generate as little waste as possible.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Social|Industry, innovation and infrastructure|Waste reduction strategies|Circular economy_qna_007
nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: How does the circular economy propose to optimize resource use according to the study?
nodes.answer: The circular economy proposes to optimize resource use by maintaining the value of products, materials, and resources in the economy for as long as possible while minimizing the intake of virgin materials and reducing waste generation.
nodes.paragraph: Through the introduction of innovative approaches, the circular economy enables employment creation and fosters economic growth and develop - ment. Significant benefits can be gained from a country implementing circular or sustainable practices, par - ticularly in terms of environmental benefits. Circular - ity helps devise effective strategies to overcome loss of resources, and emissions reduction, thereby protect - ing the ecosystem (Rizos et al., 2016). Circularity as a strategic model ensures the value of products, materi - als, and resources is maintained in the economy for as long as possible. All output from one process is input for another (see Fig. 1). Thus, a move towards a circular economy entails reducing the intake of virgin materials and reducing the generation of waste. At its core, the ethos of circularity is entrenched in the need to turn waste into wealth. The economic, environ - mental, and societal benefits of a circular economy are becoming increasingly evident. It presents businesses and governments all over the world with the potential to cre - ate an economy that is distributed, diverse, and inclusive.
